## August 24, 1931

There is no good year to be born into the Great Depression, but 1931 is a strong candidate for the worst of them. The crash had happened nearly two years before, long enough for denial to have burned off and despair to have set in. Banks were failing in cascades — Austria's Creditanstalt had collapsed in May, triggering a European banking crisis that was still propagating. Unemployment in the United States was climbing past sixteen percent and accelerating. Herbert Hoover, who had entered office in 1929 with a reputation as the most capable administrator in American public life, had deployed his considerable competence against the Depression and was losing. The rescue that would eventually come — the man who would provide it, the programs he would build — was not yet visible. Franklin Roosevelt was still the governor of New York.

**On the day you were born**, Britain's Labour government formally ended. Ramsay MacDonald — Labour prime minister, socialist by declared conviction, the first working-class politician to lead a British government — resigned under the crushing pressure of financial crisis and within hours was asked to lead a National Government coalition dominated by his political opponents. The Labour Party expelled him immediately as a traitor. MacDonald continued as prime minister, now dependent on Conservative votes, having crossed a line his movement regarded as unforgivable. It was a precise demonstration of what financial crisis does to political identity: the ground moves, and people discover they are standing somewhere they never intended to be.

**You were born in Prohibition America**, a fact now so far from living memory that it requires deliberate effort to reconstruct. The Eighteenth Amendment had been in force for eleven years. Alcohol was illegal. Al Capone — not yet convicted, still running Chicago's bootlegging operations with industrial efficiency — was at the peak of his power. Speakeasies operated openly in every American city, supplied by criminal networks that were themselves a product of the law they circumvented. The contradiction between the law as written and American behavior as lived was total, and everyone knew it. You were two years old when Prohibition was repealed, in December 1933. You were born into one legal America and grew up in another.

**Twenty-five days after your birth**, on September 18, 1931, Japanese officers staged a controlled explosion near Mukden in Manchuria, blamed Chinese saboteurs, and used the fabricated incident to launch an invasion they had planned for months. Japan would spend the next fourteen years extending this logic across Asia. The League of Nations condemned the invasion and did nothing. The international system that was supposed to prevent exactly this kind of aggression demonstrated, in that moment, that it would not. The world took note. The lesson would be applied in Ethiopia, in Spain, in the Rhineland — the entire decade of the 1930s can be read as a series of applications of what the Manchurian Incident proved.

**The rescue arrived fifteen months after your birth.** Roosevelt was inaugurated on March 4, 1933, when you were nineteen months old. His first Fireside Chat — broadcast over radio, speaking directly to American families in their living rooms — came eight days later. You were too young to remember these broadcasts as events; you grew up inside their consequences. The New Deal — the agencies, the programs, the idea that government bore responsibility for economic life — was the political environment of your entire childhood and adolescence. You did not choose it; you simply breathed it. The argument about its legacy continues.

---

**What ninety-five years looks like:**

You were born before television existed as a commercial medium, before penicillin was available as a drug, before commercial aviation connected continents. The defining technology of your early childhood was radio — a medium that required no image, only a voice. You heard the world before you saw it represented.

You were eight when Germany invaded Poland, thirteen when the war ended. Old enough to know the war completely — its absences, its rationing, its anxieties, its maps pinned to walls — but young enough to have been shielded from its worst by the adults around you and the ocean between you and it. You came of age into the postwar prosperity, which after the Depression and the war must have felt not merely comfortable but miraculous: that abundance was the default, that catastrophe was the exception.

You were twenty-eight when the Soviets launched Sputnik. Twenty-nine when Castro took Cuba. Thirty-one during the Berlin Wall's construction. Thirty-two during the Cuban Missile Crisis — at which point you were old enough to understand exactly what was at stake, having spent your entire adult life in the nuclear shadow. Thirty-seven when King and Kennedy were killed in the same spring. Thirty-eight when men walked on the Moon.

The Berlin Wall fell when you were fifty-eight. September 11 when you were seventy. COVID when you were eighty-eight.

You turned ninety-five twelve days ago. You were born when there were Americans alive who had fought in the Civil War — the last Union veteran would live until 1956, when you were twenty-five. You now live in the age of artificial intelligence that can hold a conversation, write prose, generate images, and reason through problems.

---

The distance between those two points is not merely historical. It is the distance between a world that communicated by letter and radio and a world that communicates at the speed of light to anyone anywhere. You have not observed this change from outside it; you have lived it, year by year, as the normal accumulation of a single life. That is the most remarkable thing about ninety-five years: how ordinary each year felt while it was happening, and how extraordinary the whole looks in retrospect.
